why:
Refuted on two independent grounds: it is an already-recorded deviation, and its stated mechanism is wrong.

**1. The doc sentence is real.** `curl -sL https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandbox-environments.md` line 106 carries the quote verbatim: "You can layer the built-in Bash sandbox inside the container for per-command restrictions. Unprivileged containers need the nested-sandbox setting described in [Sandboxing troubleshooting](/docs/en/sandboxing#troubleshooting)." The setting name is also correct — `sandboxing.md:458` names `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` and explains it makes "the inner sandbox bind-mount the container's existing `/proc` instead" of a fresh one.

**2. The cited code is accurate, as far as it goes.** `packages/shared/src/config/sandbox-settings.ts:172-180` — `SANDBOX_SETTING_KEYS` holds exactly seven entries (`excludedCommands`, `deniedReadRoots`, `deniedWriteRoots`, `additionalWritableRoots`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands`, `network`, `filesystem`); `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` is absent (verified `grep -ran`, zero hits anywhere in `packages/`). The precondition is present too: our bwrap invocation passes `'--proc', '/proc'` at `packages/session-tools-core/src/runtime/filesystem-isolation.ts:304` — precisely the fresh-`/proc` mount the doc says fails in an unprivileged container.

**3. THE REFUTATION — this is an already-recorded deviation, and the "OUR STATE" text is copied from our own register.** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-deviation-register.md:288` already reads: "**not implemented** — sandbox-environments.md:106 -- \"Unprivileged containers need the nested-sandbox setting\", i.e. enableWeakerNestedSandbox, which makes bubblewrap bind-mount the container's existing /proc instead of a fresh one. We have no such key: resolveLinuxIsolation fails closed with process-isolation-unavailable, so Nessy cannot run inside an unprivileged container at all." That row was harvested from `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-29-sandbox-network-enforcement.md:191` — item 5 of a nine-row list Task 3 of that plan wrote deliberately, categorising every remaining line of this exact doc page as `not implemented` or `inapplicable`. Per AGENTS.md, a plan's category string is where a deviation's reason lives. It is NOT one of the nine inert-worklist §3 owner decisions (I checked; none of the nine concerns sandboxing keys), but it is a dated, landed, generated-register entry covering this page line-for-line. Our own sweep data already says so: `docs/superpowers/specs/data/2026-07-31-doc-sweep-phase1.json:1030` notes that "`autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` and `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` … carry dated \"documented, not implemented\" decisions in the deviation register."

**4. One layer down, the mechanism is also wrong** — the "consequence is false" shape AGENTS.md warns about. `resolveLinuxIsolation` does *not* reliably "fail closed with `process-isolation-unavailable`" inside an unprivileged container. `resolveTrustedIsolationLauncher` (`packages/session-tools-core/src/runtime/trusted-isolation-launchers.ts:23-37`) is a `realpathSync` + `isFile()` + `accessSync(X_OK)` check with **no runtime probe**. So with bwrap installed — the normal case in any container image meant to sandbox — `applyFilesystemIsolation` returns `status: 'enforced'`, and the `if (filesystem.status !== 'enforced') throw` at `linux.ts:49` never fires. The plan is built and the failure lands *later, at spawn*, as bwrap's own "Can't mount proc" error, not as `process-isolation-unavailable`. Only the network leg probes at all (`usableUnsharePath` spawnSync's `unshare -n true`, `network-isolation.ts:27-31`), and even it throws only when firejail is *also* missing.

**5. Sibling-subsystem naming error.** The claim says `resolveLinuxIsolation` "builds an `unshare`/`firejail` profile". Those are the two *network* backends (`network-isolation.ts:39`). The filesystem layer — the one the doc's setting is actually about — is **bwrap-preferred**, firejail-fallback (`filesystem-isolation.ts:263, 313`). Naming unshare/firejail hides the fact that the affected component is exactly bubblewrap.
correctedState:
Accurate but already recorded, and the mechanism needs rewriting.

The key genuinely does not exist: `SANDBOX_SETTING_KEYS` (`packages/shared/src/config/sandbox-settings.ts:172-180`) has seven entries and `enableWeakerNestedSandbox` is not one of them (zero occurrences repo-wide under `grep -ran`). The condition the setting exists to fix is genuinely present: `packages/session-tools-core/src/runtime/filesystem-isolation.ts:304` passes `'--proc', '/proc'` to bwrap, the fresh-`/proc` mount that an unprivileged container refuses.

But this is `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-deviation-register.md:288`, a `documented, not implemented` row generated from `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-29-sandbox-network-enforcement.md:191`, where Task 3 deliberately categorised all nine remaining lines of `sandbox-environments.md`. A recorded decision, not a new defect.

The failure mode, corrected: `resolveLinuxIsolation` does not fail closed here. `resolveTrustedIsolationLauncher` (`trusted-isolation-launchers.ts:23-37`) only checks that the binary exists and is executable — there is no runtime probe — so with bwrap installed, `applyFilesystemIsolation` reports `status: 'enforced'`, `linux.ts:49` does not throw, and the isolated command instead dies at spawn with bwrap's own `/proc` mount error. `process-isolation-unavailable:linux:<profile>:filesystem` is raised only when neither bwrap nor firejail is installed at a trusted path. The one leg that does probe is network (`usableUnsharePath`, `network-isolation.ts:27-31`), and it throws only if firejail is missing too. So the honest statement is "a supervised session fails inside an unprivileged container with an opaque bwrap spawn error rather than a diagnosable isolation refusal" — which, if anything, is a *better* row than the one on file, and the remediation text in `isolation-remediation.ts` ("install bwrap (bubblewrap) or firejail so writes can be scoped to the workspace") would be actively misleading there, since bwrap is already installed.
